newsitem.title: UK: Sonatrach halts loading of big naphtha vessels-trade.
newsitem.headline: Sonatrach halts loading of big naphtha vessels-trade.

text.p: Algerian state oil company Sonatrach has suspended the loading of double stem naphtha cargoes out of Skikda leaving a number of traders trying to work the Asian arbitrage in the lurch, traders said on Thursday.
They said the move could have severe repercussions for the sickly European market, because it effectively closes the arbitrage door to Asia which is only open to larger, double stem cargoes.

According to trading sources who had spoken to Sonatrach, the suspension was linked to the fact that jetty number three, the only one equipped for larger cargoes, would be loading fuel oil over the next 10 days.
Traders said a 60,000 tonne vessel has been anchored outside Skikda for about four days waiting to load an Eastbound double stem of April naphtha, but loading had been delayed by bad weather.
While players had been hoping to work at least two double stems of May naphtha out of Skikda. A vessel had been fixed for one of the May cargoes, they said.
"The April double stem will be loaded, but so far Sonatrach has refused to give permission for double stem loading in May," said one trader.
"This could muck up a lot of people's plans," said another trader. "The arb's only open for bigger cargoes and if these can't load the material's stuck in Europe."

Contract holders are also annoyed by Sonatrach's decision because they say they agreed to a 75 cent premium on the contract price back in March on the proviso the company would exercise flexibility with regards to double stem loading.
"They're not doing themselves any favours," said another trader.
Sonatrach was not available for comment on the decision, and players were not expecting any response to their complaints until next week.

Although the arbitrage door will eventually reopen when European prices fall on the extra supply and Asian prices rise on the shortfall in expected cargoes, traders said exporters would then have to contend with a shortage of 25-30,000 tonne vessels available for Asian trips. -- Melanie Goodfellow, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 7714.
